The word quaver as a noun has two distinct meanings — one from the world of music, and one from everyday speech. Both are common and important to know.
Meaning 1 — In Music: A Type of Note

A quaver is a specific musical note that tells a musician how long to hold a sound. This meaning is standard in British and Commonwealth English (UK, Australia, Canada, etc.). Americans call the exact same note an eighth note, so if you've come across that term before, you already know what a quaver is.

How long does it last?

To understand its duration, start with a simple reference point. The longest common note is called a whole note. Think of it as one full unit of time. Now divide it:

  • A half note = half of a whole note
  • A quarter note = one-quarter of a whole note
  • A quaver = one-eighth of a whole note

So a quaver is quite short — it lasts only half as long as a quarter note, which is already brief. You can fit eight quavers into the time of a single whole note.

What does it look like written down?

A quaver has three parts:

  • A filled-in oval (the note head)
  • A vertical line attached to it (the stem)
  • A single curved tail (called a flag) at the top of the stem

When several quavers appear in a row, their tails are often joined together by a thick horizontal or diagonal bar called a beam. This is purely for visual convenience — it makes a group of quavers easier to read on the page. Whether the tail is free or beamed, the note lasts exactly the same amount of time.

There is also a dotted quaver, which is a quaver with a small dot placed beside the note head. That dot adds half the quaver's value to itself, making the dotted quaver last three-sixteenths of a whole note instead of one-eighth. You'll encounter this often in music.

The quaver rest

Just as every note has a matching silence of the same length, a quaver has its own rest — called a quaver rest. It tells the musician to be silent for the same duration as a quaver note. On a page of music, it looks like a small angular squiggle or a stylised number seven.

How is a quaver used in practice?

Quavers appear constantly in music because they are versatile and expressive. When a composer wants a fast, light, or busy feel, they often write quavers. Playing many quavers in a row creates a rapid, energetic effect — think of fast piano runs, a drummer keeping a steady beat, or a guitarist strumming quickly. Slow pieces use quavers too, but they feel more gentle and flowing there than rushed.

Example sentence: "The melody opened with a run of quavers that gave the passage a bright, dancing energy."
Meaning 2 — In Everyday Speech: A Trembling in the Voice

Outside of music, a quaver describes a slight, involuntary trembling or wavering quality in a person's voice. It is the subtle shake that enters someone's voice when they are gripped by a powerful emotion or when their body is physically unsteady, as can happen in old age.

What causes it?

A quaver in the voice typically arises when someone is:

  • Frightened or anxious — fear makes the voice lose its steadiness
  • Deeply sad or grieving — sorrow can cause the voice to waver or nearly break
  • Struggling not to cry — suppressing tears often produces a noticeable tremor
  • Overwhelmed, even by joy or relief — intense positive emotions can shake the voice too
  • Very elderly — the natural physical changes of old age sometimes give the voice a gentle, permanent quaver

An important detail

A quaver in the voice is almost always involuntary — the person is not choosing to make their voice shake. It happens because the emotion or physical state is so powerful that it breaks through, despite the person's best efforts to sound calm. This is what makes it so revealing and so human. When you hear a quaver in someone's voice, you instantly know that something significant is happening inside them.

How to picture it

Imagine someone calling you to share heartbreaking news. As they speak, their voice doesn't flow out smoothly and evenly — it wobbles slightly, dips unexpectedly, and sounds like it could crack into tears at any moment. That unsteady, wavering quality is exactly a quaver.

Example sentences:

  • "There was a quaver in her voice when she spoke about her late husband."
  • "He answered confidently, but I caught a slight quaver that gave away his nerves."
  • "The old soldier's voice had a gentle quaver, yet every word he spoke carried great weight."
  • "She took a breath to steady herself, but the quaver in her voice was impossible to hide."
How Are the Two Meanings Connected?

At first glance, a musical note and a shaky voice seem unrelated — but the connection is elegant. Both meanings share the idea of something brief, light, and trembling. A quaver in music is a short, flickering sound; a quaver in the voice is a brief, flickering tremor. In both cases, the word captures something delicate and wavering, rather than something solid and sustained. Once you see that thread, both meanings become easy to remember together.

Quaver (noun) has two meanings:

In music — a short note equal to one-eighth of a whole note (Americans call it an "eighth note"). It has a filled oval, a stem, and a single tail or flag. It can appear alone or beamed with other quavers. Its matching silence is a quaver rest. A dotted quaver lasts slightly longer, adding half its value to itself.

In everyday speech — a slight, involuntary trembling or wavering in a person's voice, caused by strong emotion (fear, grief, joy, etc.) or old age. It is always a signal that the person is deeply affected by something, even if they are trying to appear calm.
